title: The Worst Waiter in Cairo
teaser: Three friends, one phone and a very bad idea for a sketch.
paragraphs: Ali, Hoda and Bassem are best friends. They love funny videos, so one day they decide to make their own sketch. The idea is simple: Bassem plays the worst waiter in Cairo.

They film in Hoda’s living room. Ali is the customer. He asks for a cup of tea. Bassem brings a plate of rice. Ali asks for the bill. Bassem brings a pillow. Ali asks, “Where is my tea?” Bassem answers, “The tea is on holiday.”
They try to film it ten times, but they cannot stop laughing. Hoda’s little brother walks into the room in the middle of a scene. Her mother calls her for lunch. The phone falls on the floor twice.
Finally, they finish. The video is two minutes long. They watch it together, and they are not sure it is funny. “Maybe it is only funny for us,” says Hoda.
They post it anyway. The next day, their classmates are repeating “The tea is on holiday” in every lesson. Even the maths teacher says it. Bassem has a new nickname now: the Waiter.

a person who buys something in a shop or café

recap: Three friends film a sketch about a terrible waiter; nobody can stop laughing, and the line “The tea is on holiday” becomes famous at school.

title: Why Do We Laugh?
teaser: Laughter is older than language. Scientists think it has a job.
paragraphs: Humans laugh many times a day, but most of the time it is not because of jokes. Researchers who recorded real conversations found that people mostly laugh after ordinary sentences like “See you later” or “I know!” This suggests that laughter is more about connection than comedy.

Laughter is also very old. Chimpanzees, gorillas and even rats make laugh-like sounds when they play. Many scientists think laughter began as a signal that means “this is play, not a real fight”. It told others that it was safe to relax.

When we laugh, our body changes. Our breathing changes, many muscles move, and the brain releases chemicals that make us feel good and reduce stress. That is why laughing with friends after a hard day can feel like a small holiday.

Laughter is also contagious. When we hear someone laugh, the parts of our brain that control our own face become active, so we are more likely to laugh too. This is why TV comedy shows used recorded laughter, and why jokes are funnier in a full room.

So what makes a joke funny? One popular theory is surprise: a joke leads us to expect one thing and then gives us another, but in a way that is harmless. When the surprise is safe, we laugh. When it hurts someone, the laughter often stops.

title: Five Minutes on Stage
teaser: Mostafa is funny with his friends. Is he funny with strangers?
paragraphs: Everyone in Mostafa’s office says he is the funniest person they know. He tells stories about his crazy uncle, his noisy neighbours and his terrible cooking. So his colleagues push him: “Go to a comedy night!”

There is a comedy night every Wednesday in a small theatre in Downtown. New comedians can have five minutes on stage. Mostafa signs up. For two weeks, he writes jokes on his phone and practises in front of the mirror.

On Wednesday, he is the sixth comedian. The first five are very good, and the audience is laughing a lot. When the host calls his name, Mostafa walks to the microphone. His first joke is about his uncle. Nobody laughs.

His face is hot. He forgets his second joke. Then he says, honestly, “I am very nervous. My uncle would be proud of this disaster.” The audience laughs, a big real laugh. Mostafa relaxes and tells the rest of his stories like he does at the office.
When he finishes, people clap. Backstage, an older comedian tells him, “Your best joke was the true one. Write more true jokes.” Mostafa goes home and opens his phone. He has a lot of true stories.

a person who makes people laugh on stage
to put your name on a list to do something

recap: Mostafa tries a comedy night; his first joke fails, but being honest about his nerves makes the audience laugh, and he learns to write true jokes.

title: How a Stand-up Joke Is Built
teaser: Set-up, punchline, tag. Comedy has more engineering than you think.
paragraphs: A good stand-up set looks natural, as if the comedian is just chatting with the audience. In reality, most professional comedians rewrite and test each joke dozens of times before it feels effortless.

The basic structure has two parts. The set-up gives the audience a situation and makes them expect something. The punchline breaks that expectation in a surprising way. The bigger the gap between what we expect and what we get, the stronger the laugh, as long as it still makes sense.

Many comedians add tags: extra punchlines after the first one, using the same set-up. A tag lets the comedian get two or three laughs from one situation without starting again. Callbacks are similar: a reference later in the show to an earlier joke, which feels like a shared secret with the audience.

Timing matters a lot. A short pause before the punchline builds tension; speaking too quickly can kill a joke. Comedians also choose words carefully, often putting the funniest word at the very end of a sentence so the laugh comes at the right moment.

New material is usually tested at open mic nights. If a joke gets no laugh, the comedian changes a word, cuts a sentence or moves the punchline, and tries again next week. A ten-minute set can take months to build. The goal is to make all that work invisible.

recap: Stand-up jokes use set-ups, punchlines, tags, callbacks and careful timing; comedians test and rewrite them at open mics for months.

title: Reacting to Grandma
teaser: Rana started a reaction channel. Her best guest was seventy-five.
paragraphs: Rana loves reaction videos. She watches people react to music, films and strange internet trends. One day, she decides to start her own channel. But what can she react to that is different?
Then she has an idea. Her grandmother, Teta Fatma, is seventy-five and has never used TikTok. Rana sits next to her on the sofa and shows her popular videos. She films Teta’s reactions.

Teta’s reactions are amazing. She does not understand dance challenges. “Why is this boy jumping in the kitchen?” she asks. When she sees a cooking video, she says the cook is using too much oil. When she hears a new rap song, she starts to clap to the beat.
Rana posts the first video. People love Teta. They write comments like, “I want a grandma like this!” and “Teta for president!” Soon, people send suggestions for the next videos.

Now, every Friday, Rana and Teta film a new episode. Teta still does not use social media. But when someone recognises her at the market and asks for a selfie, she fixes her scarf and smiles like a star.

recap: Rana films her 75-year-old grandmother reacting to internet videos; the funny reactions become a popular weekly series.

title: Why Do We Watch Other People Watching?
teaser: Reaction videos sound strange. Millions love them anyway.
paragraphs: Describe a reaction video to someone who has never seen one, and it sounds odd: you watch a person watching something else. Yet reaction channels have millions of subscribers. Why?

One reason is shared emotion. Humans are social, and many experiences feel bigger when we share them. Watching a trailer or a football goal alone can feel flat; seeing someone scream with excitement makes it more fun, almost like watching with a friend.

Another reason is curiosity about other people. Reaction videos often show someone experiencing something for the first time: a teacher reacting to slang, foreigners trying Egyptian food, or older people hearing modern music. We enjoy their surprise and compare it with our own first time.

Some reactions are educational. A vocal coach reacting to a singer explains techniques you would never notice. A doctor reacting to a medical drama tells you what is realistic and what is not. In these videos, the reactor is really a guide.

There is also a debate about fairness. Some creators complain that reactors use their videos, get the views and add very little. Platforms have rules about fair use, and many respected reactors now add a lot of commentary, pause often and link to the original creator.

recap: People watch reactions for shared emotion, curiosity and expert explanations; fairness to original creators is an ongoing debate.

title: The Kind Prank
teaser: Their pranks made people angry. Then they tried a different kind.
paragraphs: Seif and Hamza have a prank channel. In their old videos, they scared people in the street with fake spiders and loud noises. Some people laughed, but many were angry. One man almost fell down the stairs. After that video, they felt bad.
“We need a new idea,” says Hamza. “Pranks that make people happy, not scared.” Seif thinks for a long time. Then he smiles. “What if we surprise people with something nice?”

Their first kind prank is at a bus stop. Seif pretends to be a lost tourist and asks a young woman for directions. When she helps him, Hamza appears with flowers and a sign that says, “Thank you for being kind!”

Next, they go to a small bakery. They buy all the bread and ask the baker to give it free to the next customers. The baker’s face when people say, “It’s already paid for!” is the best part of the video.

The new videos get more views than the old ones. But the best part is the comments. People write about kind things they did that day. Seif reads them every night. “This is better,” he says. “Much better.”

title: When Online Challenges Go Wrong
teaser: Some challenges raise money for charity. Others send people to hospital.
paragraphs: An online challenge is simple: someone does something unusual, films it, and invites others to copy it. The best challenges spread fast because they are easy to join, fun to watch and give people a reason to tag their friends.

Some challenges have done a lot of good. Around 2014, millions of people poured ice water over their heads and donated money to research into a serious disease. The challenge raised over one hundred million dollars in a few months and helped fund important scientific discoveries.

Other challenges are dangerous. Some have encouraged people to eat things that are not food, hold their breath until they faint, or jump from moving cars. Young people are especially at risk, partly because the part of the brain that judges risk is still developing in teenagers, and partly because social approval feels extremely important at that age.

Platforms try to respond. They remove dangerous videos, show warning messages when someone searches for a harmful challenge, and sometimes block certain hashtags. But new challenges appear faster than rules can follow.

A useful question before joining any challenge is: “Would I do this if nobody was filming?” If the honest answer is no, the risk is probably not worth a few likes. And if a friend tags you in something dangerous, it is completely fine to say no.

recap: Online challenges spread easily; some raised money for research, others caused injuries; asking “Would I do this without a camera?” helps.

title: The Podcast in the Car
teaser: Two brothers stuck in traffic every day decided to record it.
paragraphs: Every morning, Adel and his younger brother Khaled drive from Sheikh Zayed to their jobs in Cairo. The traffic is terrible. The trip takes ninety minutes. They are bored, so they talk about everything: football, food, their family and their strange dreams.
One day, Khaled says, “Our conversations are funnier than many podcasts. Let’s record them.” Adel laughs, but he agrees. They put a small microphone on the dashboard.
Their first episode is not great. You can hear car horns all the time, and Adel forgets that people are listening. But a few friends listen to it and ask for more.

They start to plan a little. Each episode has a topic, like “The worst wedding we went to” or “Things our mother says.” They ask listeners to send questions. Some listeners send voice messages from their own cars.

After one year, the podcast has thousands of listeners. People call it “the traffic podcast.” The brothers still drive the same road every day. But now, when the traffic is very bad, Khaled smiles and says, “Good. More time to record.”

title: Why Do People Listen to Three-Hour Podcasts?
teaser: In the age of 15-second videos, long talks are booming. Here’s why.
paragraphs: Attention spans are supposedly getting shorter, and many apps are built around videos under a minute long. At the same time, some of the most popular shows in the world are podcasts where two people talk for two or three hours. How can both be true?

One answer is that podcasts fit into time we already have. People listen while driving, cooking, cleaning or going to the gym. A podcast does not need your eyes, so it fills moments that a video cannot.

Long conversations also feel more real. In a short interview, guests often repeat prepared answers. After an hour, they relax, make jokes, tell personal stories and sometimes change their minds. Many listeners say they feel they really know the hosts, almost like friends. Researchers call this a parasocial relationship: a one-sided connection with someone who does not know you.

For learners of English, long podcasts are a powerful tool. You hear natural speech, real pauses, slang and different accents. Because the topic continues for a long time, you have many chances to understand words from context.

The trick is to choose a topic you genuinely enjoy, start with hosts who speak clearly, and not worry about understanding everything. If you follow the main idea and enjoy it, your brain is already learning.
